title: Delegates and Events
description: Learn about delegates and events for event-driven programming in C#.

data.text: **Delegates** are type-safe function pointers, and **events** build on delegates to implement the publisher-subscriber pattern. Together they enable loose coupling and event-driven architecture in C#.

A delegate defines the signature of a method. You can create an instance of a delegate and point it to any method with a matching signature. Delegates are the foundation of callbacks, LINQ, and events in C#.

A delegate that holds references to multiple methods. Invoking it calls all methods in order.

data.text: You can combine multiple method references into a single delegate using the `+` operator. When invoked, each method runs in order. Use `-=` to remove a handler.

data.title: Multicast Delegate
Multicast Return Values
data.text: If a multicast delegate has a return type, only the last handler's return value is preserved. Multicast delegates are best used with void return types.
C# provides three commonly used generic delegates so you rarely need to declare custom ones.

data.text: An event is a mechanism for a class to notify other classes when something happens. The declaring class raises the event; subscribers attach handlers. Events use delegates internally but expose only `+=` and `-=` operations, protecting the invocation list from external tampering.

data.text: The .NET Framework provides `EventHandler` and `EventHandler<TEventArgs>` as standard delegate types for events. Using them keeps your code consistent with the rest of the ecosystem.

data.title: Standard .NET Event Pattern
Stock Ticker
Protected virtual OnEventName Pattern
data.text: Declare a protected virtual method named OnEventName to raise events. This allows derived classes to override the raising behavior without directly accessing the event.
Always unsubscribe from events when you no longer need them, especially in long-lived publishers. Failing to do so can prevent garbage collection of subscribers, causing memory leaks.

items.question: What is the difference between a delegate and an event?
items.answer: A delegate is a type-safe function pointer. An event is a wrapper around a delegate that restricts external code to only subscribe or unsubscribe; only the declaring class can invoke (raise) the event.

items.question: When should I use multicast delegates?
items.answer: Use multicast delegates when multiple subscribers need to react to the same action, such as logging, validation pipelines, or notification systems. Keep handlers void-returning for predictable behavior.

items.question: What causes event memory leaks?
items.answer: If a publisher holds a strong reference to subscriber handlers and the publisher outlives the subscriber, the subscriber cannot be garbage collected. Always unsubscribe in Dispose or use weak-event patterns for long-lived publishers.

items.question: Are events the same as async/await?
items.answer: No. Events are synchronous notifications by default. You can call async methods inside event handlers, but the event itself does not await them. For true asynchronous messaging, consider channels or reactive extensions.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Multicast delegates call multiple methods in order
Action, Func, and Predicate are built-in delegates
Events encapsulate delegates for safe publish-subscribe
Always unsubscribe to avoid memory leaks
data.takeaway: Delegates and events enable clean, decoupled communication between components.
